title: Fallback Amplification Postmortem + Containment Plan
summary: Postmortem discussing an incident where Redwood fallbacks amplified load onto slower dedicated pools during a traffic spike, causing increased latencies and partial timeouts for AstraLogistics. The call reviewed timelines, root causes (misrouted fallbacks + lack of backpressure on slowpath), mitigations (rate-limited fallback, circuit-breaker, pre-warm strategy, telemetry enrichment), and an initial containment plan with owners and dates.
action_items: Maya Chen - run a focused load test to reproduce fallback-amplification pattern and capture KV cache metrics - due 2025-12-17
Priya Singh - enable request-level tracing (sampled) for fallback path and forward logs to Redwood debug bucket - due 2025-12-15
Jordan Patel - share containment playbook and config patch to rate-limit fallback calls, plus rollback steps - due 2025-12-12
Noah Rivera - schedule a 1-hr run of joint smoke tests with Astra dev and ops teams after patch applied - due 2025-12-19
Evan Li - confirm legal/ops approval for increasing logging retention by 7 days for incident analysis - due 2025-12-14
next_steps: Redwood to deliver a hotfix branch that adds fallback rate limit and a conservative circuit-breaker policy
Customer to enable richer traces on representative traffic and share sample logs
Joint load test to be executed in staging with controlled traffic ramp to validate containment
Follow-up meeting in one week to review test results and agree on long-term roadmap
meeting_header: Date: 2025-12-10 | Start: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 48m | Location: Zoom | Recording: yes | Transcript generated by Fireflies.ai
questions: What caused fallbacks to be routed to the slowpath rather than throttled?
Can we short-circuit sub-second errors before invoking heavy KV lookups?
How much telemetry do we need to capture to reproduce behavior?
Is there an acceptable guardrail for extra latency during business-critical windows?
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh this is the Astra + Redwood postmortem for the fallback amplification incident. We'll go quickly through timeline, then root cause, then containment.
[00:18] Carlos Mendez: Thanks Jordan. We'll try to keep it tight, we had a pretty bad customer impact yesterday morning, so appreciate the quick sync.
[00:31] Priya Singh: Quick note — our alerts showed a spike at 09:11 and timeouts at the edge, then a cascade into longer latencies in dedicated pools.
[00:45] Maya Chen: Right, and to be precise the majority of the increased traffic was routed to the so-called slow-path — internal name was slowpool-3 — which wasn't pre-warmed and had longer cold-start-ish behavior, plus heavy KV activity.
[01:02] Evan Li: Can you explain slowpath vs fastpath again? We use both dedicated and hosted in prod for different tenants.
[01:15] Maya Chen: Sure, fastpath is our low-latency shard on curated models with aggressive pooling; slowpath is either capacity-optimized quantized variants or fallback when fastpath signals capacity shortage. In this incident a fallback rule routed at 5% failure rate, but it escalated.
[01:34] Priya Singh: The problem is the fallback didn't have any form of backpressure, so as requests were diverted they triggered heavier KV cache reads and increased the slowpath cpu/GPU queue, which slowed down the slowpath and produced more fallbacks from other fastpath requests — a positive feedback loop.
[02:05] Jordan Patel: So the amplification is basically a loop: fallback routing -> slowpath overload -> slowpath latency -> fastpath sees apparent failures -> more fallbacks.
[02:20] Leah O'Connor: We also saw more 503s at our API gateway, customers seeing partial responses.
[02:30] Carlos Mendez: We have a couple of big job windows in the morning, that increased baseline. That weekend traffic pattern plus a deploy coincided.
[02:44] Maya Chen: Yeah deploy noise likely lowered fastpath headroom. We should flag deployments during heavy windows.
[03:00] Priya Singh: Telemetry gap — we didn't have request-level trace ids across the handoff, so it's hard to reconstitute the exact call path for many requests.
[03:12] Jordan Patel: Agreed, that's on us to propose a tracing patch.
[03:20] -- discussion moves to containment --
[03:30] Jordan Patel: Short-term containment options we discussed: 1) add conservative rate-limit on fallback path, 2) introduce circuit-breaker that opens if slowpath P95 > threshold, 3) pre-warm a minimal slowpath pool during business windows, 4) short-circuit expensive KV lookups for sampling responses.
[03:55] Evan Li: Which of these can you deliver quickly?
[04:00] Maya Chen: Rate-limit + circuit-breaker are config changes we can ship as a hotfix in ~24-48 hours. Pre-warm is org-level but doable in a week. KV short-circuit needs product signoff.
[04:16] Priya Singh: We'd prefer a quick config change and then a joint test. Also, we need to confirm SSO and RBAC for debug access so our SREs can see traces.
[04:30] Jordan Patel: We'll provide a temporary debug bucket and grant scoped access.
[04:36] -- timestamped technical deep-dive --
[05:00] Maya Chen: Looking at the traces we managed to capture, the KV cache lookups were causing 45-120ms tails on the slowpath plus queueing delays. Also some model variants on slowpath load additional helpers that amplify latency.
[05:30] Carlos Mendez: Our middleware retries at the client level sometimes. That increased reissue to backend.
[05:45] Leah O'Connor: Right, the client retries turned a single slow event into multiple concurrent requests, exacerbating the loop. We should coordinate retry policies.
[06:05] Maya Chen: Good catch — we should recommend a jittered retry with exponential backoff and a lower retry ceiling for endpoints with potential KV dependency.
[06:22] Priya Singh: About telemetry: we will enable trace sampling at 10% for fallback paths, and keep full logs for any error > 500 for 7 days. Is that acceptable?
[06:36] Jordan Patel: Yes, Redwood will accept those logs and help analyze; we also suggest adding a lightweight request tag to identify slowpath invocations.
[06:48] Evan Li: Security concern — how do we handle PII within logs? We need redaction and KMS controls.
[07:00] Noah Rivera: We'll apply our standard redaction pipeline and use customer KMS for any sensitive artifacts; we'll share the SOC2 redaction guideline doc.
[07:12] Carlos Mendez: What about autoscaling thresholds? Was there any weird behavior there?
[07:20] Maya Chen: Autoscaler was healthy, but scale-up takes time; the amplification happened faster than scaling could react. That's why pre-warm and proactive capacity reservations during peak windows is on the table.
[07:35] Priya Singh: Action item: we need a short-term throttle on fallback at the edge.
[07:40] Jordan Patel: I'll push the rate-limit patch with a conservative default of 10 RPS per tenant to slowpath and an emergency toggle.
[07:50] Leah O'Connor: Can you also add a canary so we don't accidentally block all fallback traffic?
[07:55] Maya Chen: Yep canary with 5% roll is straightforward.
[08:05] -- misc clarifications and occasional crosstalk --
[08:20] Priya Singh: There's also the issue of client-side retries as noted; we'll patch client library to honor Retry-After and lower concurrent in-flight requests.
[08:32] Jordan Patel: We'll coordinate a release window.
[08:40] Carlos Mendez: On longer-term hardening, what do you recommend?
[08:44] Maya Chen: Long-term: robust circuit-breakers with scoring, smarter routing that factors in queue depths and real-time telemetry, KV cache redesign to avoid heavy synchronous reads on slowpath, and improved observability (end-to-end traces and synthetic tests for fallback scenarios).
[09:05] Evan Li: KV cache redesign sounds heavy; what's a pragmatic first step?
[09:10] Maya Chen: Start with asynchronous reads with best-effort results and fallback to stale caches rather than blocking; plus prioritize lightweight model variants for fallback.
[09:23] Carlos Mendez: We also want explicit SLA language for fallback behavior during incidents.
[09:28] Jordan Patel: We can suggest an addendum for our enterprise contract that defines fallback latency windows and mitigation commitments. Noah can follow-up.
[09:36] Noah Rivera: I'll own the contract note and circle back with legal.
[09:40] -- recap and owners --
[09:45] Jordan Patel: Quick recap: Redwood will deliver rate-limit + circuit-breaker hotfix, provide debug bucket and scoped access, run joint load test, and propose long-term hardening roadmap. Astra will enable tracing, reduce client retries, and approve logging retention. Owners and due dates in action items.
[10:05] Priya Singh: Thanks all, we'll aim to apply the hotfix tomorrow in staging.
[10:12] Leah O'Connor: Please include a short ops playbook for on-call to follow if we see re-amplification.
[10:18] Jordan Patel: Will do. Thanks everyone.
[10:22] -- meeting closed --
notes: Containment plan prioritized: 1) rate-limit fallbacks, 2) open circuit-breaker on P95/SLO breach, 3) staged pre-warm policy, 4) client retry dampening; telemetry patch and runbook to follow. Legal/KMS/PII considerations raised for logs.
